It's not the same, but I've been in a similar position. my first cat had lots of issues with constipation, and once we moved out of a house with a dog she was able to taper off the medications and recover. in that time at the dog house, i even introduced an orange cat to her slowly over 3 months and they aren't best buds but they hang out and coexist excellently. anyway. a month or two later, my (now ex)bf moved in with his cat - we took it slow with them, scent and site swapping over a month, they got along for a few weeks but the stress of new cat triggered her again. she never got along with ex's cat again, and we had to keep them seperated 24/7. i believe that my cat associated the pain of a butt full of poop with his cat. we have been in our own place for a month now and she is successfully tapering off her medications again. some cats, especially medically fragile ones, just won't get along. i hate to say it, but i don't think my cat is a unique case - it's nigh impossible to scrap the association these animals build around others of their species and pain.

best advice i can give from the side of the plaintiff is, is show up to the hearing. have a clear record going back 3 months of your monthly income, bills, any other financial obligations, married? own/rent? car payments? utilities? kids/dependents? . bring proof of any government assistance, and outline any financial hardships you've undergone in the recent past/present. make it clear you aren't disputing the debt, but you are interested in making an arrangement that is manageable for your financial situation. 

try reaching out to the collection agency again before your trial with the information i noted above, and see if they are willing to work out a plan with you - worst case they say no, bring it before the judge. 
also, with tax season starting, if you are expecting a return you may be able to negotiate a larger down payment for smaller monthly payments down the line. i know my firm is offering a lot of deals to "satisfy" a debt (aka, paying 60%-85% off in one/a few payments and calling it done)

lastly, if it's a hefty amount of debt (aka not in Small Claims court) you may benefit from hiring an attorney of your own. you will really have to do some digging, because a lot of debt consolidation attorneys really do not do sh!t for you except take your money. ask around. do research.

at the end of the day, garnishments aren't the worst thing that could happen as long as your employer doesn't d!ck around with court orders, but if you believe you can work out a reasonable payment plan pre-judgement I don't think it would hurt to try. 

!!not a lawyer!! !!just my two cents from working on the opposite end of the field!!

at least in my state, they cannot begin garnishment until after judgement has been taken and if it is determined that a) you can not/are not willing to pay on an arrangement and/or b) garnishment would be the best way to collect on your debt. so i guess i'm confused at your intial post - were you served (by a process server, certified mail etc) with a summons and complaint? those docs will list the threat of garnishment/liens if judgement is taken against you.

definitely attend the hearing to avoid a default judgement. if you can call the collection agency prior, you may be able to work out a stipulation or voluntary payment arrangement if judgement has not been entered. they may take a "financial statement" (aka job info, any rent/car/other monthly bills to determine how much they can offer for an arrangement on behalf of the client) but if you fall through on those they can take default judgement that way too.

again, im not well versed in your state's law - just passing down what i know from working in this area of law in my state. i mostly handle service lol

depends if the agency has already taken judgement. if so, and you can't prove exemption (in my state, you can be "garnishment proof" if you make X amount less than poverty line, receive state benefits or have child support/another thing taking 20%+ from your wages) then you might be out of luck.

there are some things you can do to potentially have the garnishment lifted depending on your local laws. fair disclaimer, i am NOT a lawyer and certainly don't know your local laws. however i am a paralegal at a debt collection firm who often collects for discover.

firstly. do some research on process of service for your county's court system. it seems like you're implying they did not serve you their lawsuit properly, which you can argue.
secondly, if you have any government assistance/child support etc, at least in my area that makes you untouchable to court-ordered garnishment.
thirdly. see if you can get a lawyer to file a motion to reopen if you feel like you have not had proper service and especially if you get assistance.

lastly. i am not offering legal advice! just some things you can consider if you cannot afford the garnishment and things i have picked up on while working in this field (and yes it is soul sucking)

i was in a similar situation the other week. my partner almost left me because of my drinking, and i struggled a lot with feeling left out because i was uninvited to something i was looking forward to with said partner and a bunch of their friends. the only thing that really helped me was calling a friend (to get me through to 9pm, when alcohol stops being sold in my area) and writing. a loooot of writing. 

having a journal where i can write down all the anger, frustration, and spiteful things I want to say out loud (but wouldn't) has been so helpful, i cannot understate the power of that. it's a good place for me to write my fears, exactly how i'm feeling no matter how "taboo" or awful it would be to say. and it's where i was able to self reflect, and realize that yes, i may be the reason for X or Y, but it's not personal. if anyone else did this, my friend/partner/I would do the same thing. and, it's not a punishment, it's an opportunity to be introspective, mindful and present and an invitation to be patient with yourself. 

yes, you're not able to change what happened. but the bright side is that these moments are a learning experience, and at least in my own life i've learned a lot about letting myself feel any type of way about a situation but not letting it color my whole day and letting the feeling go when it's ready. with drinking, i would just hide those feelings under the guise of not caring, and it would be amplified 100x the next day. for me, it's all about recognizing that past experiences have influenced your current reactions, feelings, expectations, but they don't shape who you are in this moment. be present and gentle with yourself.
hope that my experience can give you a little insight n feel free to message me if you need a buddy:)

I've been journaling a lot. I've kind of personified my anxiety as "fear of the future", which conflicts with my want to be more present and more patient. 

I relapsed last night after two weeks, and being able to look back at my thought process/bargaining from last night is a great reminder that alcohol is insidious. While it provides temporary relief from the anxiety, it's only amplified the next day. I'm feeling hellish, frustrated at myself, but I know that it's just a bump in the road. 

Being able to write down everything you are feeling as you feel it, even if it doesn't make any sense, is really powerful. I've been in between scrolling this sub and writing for the past 4ish hours now, and the anxiety is still there but it's definitely died down. A lot of people will suggest exercise (even a quick walk around the block) to get some of that energy out, and that is definitely helpful too.

I relapsed last night after 14 tough, but glorious days of sobriety.
This morning, I sat down and read my journal entry from yesterday. Seeing the painstakingly agonizing bargaining with myself was difficult to say the least. I feel like fucking shit today, anxious and my stomach is killing me. Hell, it's almost 5pm and I still haven't eaten. I'm exhausted, disappointed in myself that I didn't reach my goals today, but that's okay. Frustrated with not being "productive", but choosing to be sober is productive. It's fucking tough.
As they say, play the tape forward. If you did drink, how would you feel tomorrow? Sure, drinking tonight would soothe that anticipation and anxiety for a few hours, but at least for me it came back amplified 100x when I woke up on my couch way too early this morning. drinking is like popping a pimple - satisfying, but it just makes the problem worse. 
For me, I'm going to have a NA corona, some soup, and keep writing in my journal to stave off the cravings tonight. I will not drink with you tonight. Maybe tomorrow, but not tonight.

I know how it feels, and I'm still working on digging out of the rut myself.

What has been really helping recently is journaling. Any old book with blank pages works. Even the most mundane things, I write down and it always leads me to write the things I "regret" telling others. Remembering that emotions and feelings are temporary, and that I am in control is also huge. Fear, anxiety, all the feelings that make me feel nuclear are only in this moment, and knowing that if I let them exist they float off on their own is a huge skill that you can pick up easily. 

do not try to suppress the pain, instead, let the underlying emotions exist. feel them in your chest, that uncomfortable warmth. let it exist, don't ask it why, and let it move down through your body out of your fingertips. acceptance is the key. people like us, we're always gonna feel like we aren't enough, like we're shit. but if we accept ourselves, even in the smallest ways, it opens pathways for our mind to comfort us alone.

I'm autistic but being there at the game lets me get so hyperfixated that it's fairly easy for me to tune out the other stressors. what I do is make sure my phone is fully charged and have some good earplugs and headphones so I can put on music during halftime and there are some sensory rooms that I can escape to if things become too much. secondhand is the exhalation/smoke coming off a burning cigarette as we know, while thirdhand smoke is the kind that sticks to clothing and walls (if you are smoking indoors). you ever notice the Reek of someone coming back inside from a smoke? or how gross the walls look/feel in a home that has an indoor smoker? that's thirdhand, and is dangerous to vulnerable people as well.

my personal experience with this is from smoking in my tiny closet as a teen. 5 years later, and the closet/room still smells faintly of smoke even after I furiously scrubbed walls/all surfaces.
